author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The confidence which the Directory has shown me under all circumstances renders it my duty to inform them of all my actions. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Le Tourneur from Paris, 1796-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" The General-in-chief Bonaparte reviewed the looth demi-brigade, &c. He is satisfied with the appearance of the troops, their sentiments of devotion towards the Republic, and their resolution to conquer. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from -Zzth, 1796-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “16 Ventose, year 4 [March 6, 1796]. The Executive Directory addresses to you herewith, eitizen-general, the instructions which it has drawn up for the conduct of the ensuing campaign in Italy. […]”
archive: Secret letters from Napoleon's cabinet (London, 1846), Vol. I — public domain
context: The Directory's Italy instructions: seize Savona if useful; spare Genoa. Incoming voice: Paris orders to its general.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I had Barras inform the Directory of my marriage to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Barras told: married to Citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'avais chargé le citoyen Barras d'instruire le Directoire exécutif de mon mariage avec la citoyenne Tascher Beauharnais.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter received. I dined today with General Schérer and your wife. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Dined with Schérer and your wife; glad to oblige her. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu votre lettre. J'ai diné aujourd'hui chez le général Schérer avec votre femme.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers, you are naked, ill-fed; the Government owes you much and can give you nothing. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Nus, mal nourris: the most famous proclamation of the age. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Soldats, vous êtes nus, mal nourris; le Gouvernement vous doit beaucoup, il ne peut rien vous donner.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed the cavalry movement state; regiments arrive daily. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cavalry movement states; regiments arriving daily. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint l'état du mouvement de la cavalerie; vous y verrez qu'il arrive des régiments.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall be charmed to be of service to her It is said that the Genoese offer us 3,000,000 francs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Faypoult from 27M, 1796-03-27. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Warmly received by the army, whose confidence obliges my liveliest gratitude. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Well received by the army; Schérer pure and enlightened. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai été très-bien reçu par l'armée, qui me montre une confiance qui m'oblige à une vive reconnaissance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 209th's 3rd battalion stands guilty of disobedience and mutiny. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 209th refuses to march: disobedience and mutiny. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le 3e bataillon de la 209e demi-brigade s'est rendu coupable de désobéissance et d'esprit de mutinerie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The cavalry divides in two divisions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cavalry in two divisions: hussars, chasseurs assigned. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La cavalerie sera partagée en deux divisions.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Parra will at once requisition Antibes' administrators. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Antibes communes to furnish momentary supplies. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général de brigade Parra de requérir sur-le-champ les corps administratifs de cette commune.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief reviewed the 100th and 165th demi-brigades. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Reviewed 100th, 165th and Montfernie battalion. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a passé la revue de la 100e demi-brigade et de la 165e.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tonight deliver the staff officers' roll marching on the 12th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Tonight: staff, artillery and engineers lists for the 12th. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous me remettrez ce soir l'état nominatif des officiers de l'état-major qui partent le 12.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Adjutant-General Chabran leaves Nice today for Albenga post-haste. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Chabran to Albenga post-haste, 11 Germinal. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné à l'adjudant général Chabran de partir de Nice aujourd'hui pour se rendre le plus promptement à Albenga.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “One for 172,800 francs, drawn on Cadiz, has just been returned, which augments our difficulties. *' I found this army not only destitute of everything, but without discipline and in a chronic state of insubordination. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from ^^ Albenga, 1796-04-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal from you that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Director Carnot from ^' Carcare, 1796-04-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force. The enemy possesses strong places and a numerous and efficient artillery […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from *' Carru, 1796-04-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have learned with pain that our troops allowed themselves to be surprised yesterday at the village of St. Michel. […] You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received; it will only be the prelude to our victory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Eve of Montenotte: a check at San Michele, answered with a promise of revenge. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Michel By these various movements you will be in a position to take your revenge in a brilliant fashion You must not be astonished, my dear general, at the little check you have received; it will only be the prelude to our victory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Serurier from 2Qth, 1796-04-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief renews orders to hasten the new organisation. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Hasten the new organisation work in every division. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef renouvelle l'ordre d'accélérer le travail relatif à la nouvelle organisation.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A 400-sack contribution levied on Oneille valley. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 400 sacks on Oneille valley, 200 on the district. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne une contribution de quatre cents sacs dans la vallée d'Oneille.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Convene a Nice military commission for émigré Moulin, taken at Ormea. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Émigré Moulin to military commission at Nice. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous voudrez bien faire réunir une commission militaire à Nice pour y juger l'émigré Moulin, pris à Ormea.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have transferred my head-quarters to Albenga. The movement which I found commenced against Genoa has drawn the enemy out of his winter quarters. Beaulieu has published a manifesto, to which I shall reply after the battle. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Headquarters moved up; Genoa's alarm spoiled his plan to catch Beaulieu napping. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Distress has authorised insubordination, and without discipline victory is out of the question. I hope all this will be changed in the course of a few days. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Albenga, 1796-04-06. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Raise a Laigueglia–Pietra brigade for carts, forage, hospitals. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Mule brigades Laigueglia–Pietra for forage and hospitals. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous donnerez les ordres pour qu'il soit levé, pour les charrois, fourrages et hôpitaux, une brigade de Laigueglia à Pietra.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Reviewed the 39th and 69th with published satisfaction. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 39th and 69th reviewed with published satisfaction. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a passé la revue des 39e et 69e demi-brigades, avec satisfaction publiée par la voie de l'ordre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Levy two hundred mules at Pieve, Ormea and Garessio for food. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Two hundred mules at Pieve, Ormea, Garessio for food. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous donnerez l'ordre pour que l'on lève à Pieve, Ormea et Garessio, une division de deux cents mulets, pour les vivres.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, an émigré is a parricidal son no rank can sanctify; yours dishonour your army. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: An émigré is a parricidal son; his presence dishonours your army. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Monsieur, un émigré est un fils parricide qu'aucun caractère ne peut rendre sacré; ceux qui sont dans votre armée la déshonorent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I learn Genoa molests patriots and troubles France's friends. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Genoa molests patriots while sheltering émigrés. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'apprends que le Gouvernement de Gênes moleste les patriotes et inquiète les amis de la France.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Hold your troops ready to march at first signal, food issued. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Troops ready to march at first signal, with food issued. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous donne l'ordre de tenir les troupes prêtes à marcher au premier signal, avec les vivres distribués.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Augereau marches two demi-brigades and four squadrons to Mallare. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Two demi-brigades and four squadrons to Mallare by shortest road. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Augereau partira avec ses deux demi-brigades et quatre escadrons pour Mallare par le plus court chemin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Finale's artillery marches with 8-pounder, 4s, howitzer and all munitions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: 8-pounder, two 4s, howitzer, two 3s: march with all munitions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné à l'officier d'artillerie à Finale de partir avec la pièce de 8, deux pièces de 4, un obusier et toutes ses munitions.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Italian campaign has commenced. I have forwarded a report on the battle of Montenotte. After manoeuvring for three days in order to conceal his intentions, Beaulieu attacked the right of our army with 10,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: First victory dispatch: Montenotte, three days of manoeuvre. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find the details of the battles of Montenotte and Millesimo in the report forwarded to the Directory. I cannot conceal from you that I am seconded neither by the artillery nor the engineers, as, in spite of your orders, I have not a single one of the officers I asked for. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Montenotte–Millesimo (12–14 Apr). Fighting Paris as well as Piedmont: no engineers, no artillery officers sent. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “An hour after noon he attacked the redoubt of Monte Legino, which was our last line of defence. The enemy returned several times to the charge, but the redoubt, defended by 1,500 men, was rendered impregnable by the courage of those who defended it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from * Carcare, 1796-04-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The soldier without bread is driven to commit acts which make one blush to be a man. […] I have 100,000 men against me, and can oppose only 34,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry to that force. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content after Mondovi (21–22 Apr). Mondovi report: the army he found — without bread, without discipline — and made examples. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance. French original verified in the Second Empire Correspondance, Vol. I (Paris, 1858) — public domain.
originalText: Le soldat sans pain se porte à des excès de fureur qui font rougir d'être homme. […] Je ramènerai l'ordre, ou je cesserai de commander à ces brigands. J'ai 100,000 hommes contre moi, qui n'en ai que 34,000 d'infanterie et 3,500 de cavalerie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. Everything is going on well. There is not so much pillaging. The first thirst of an army in want of everything has been quenched. There was an excuse for these unfortunate fellows who after having sighed for three years on the summit of the Alps, reached the promised land and desired to enjoy it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Pillage punished: three shot, hard labour. Order before politics. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Destitute of everything, you have supplied everything. You have won battles without cannon, crossed rivers without bridges, made forced marches without shoes, bivouacked without brandy and often without bread. […] Friends, I promise you this conquest; but one condition you must swear to fulfil: respect the peoples you deliver. Else you will not be the liberators of peoples, but their scourge. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: The Cherasco proclamation, in French at last: destitute of everything, supplied everything. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Dénués de tout, vous avez suppléé à tout. Vous avez gagné des batailles sans canons, passé des rivières sans ponts, fait des marches forcées sans souliers, bivouaqué sans eau-de-vie et souvent sans pain. […] Amis, je vous la promets cette conquête; mais il est une condition qu'il faut que vous juriez de remplir: respecter les peuples que vous délivrez. Sans cela, vous ne seriez pas les libérateurs des peuples, vous en seriez les fléaux.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In three days discipline will be severely established, and astonished Italy will admire the moderation of our army as it already admires its courage. This occasions me a great deal of pain, and makes me pass very unhappy moments. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 26M, 1796-04-26. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The village of Coni has been occupied by our troops. I feel sure that you will approve of the suspension of arms granted to the Sardinians; it is an armistice accorded to one wing of an army, giving me time to beat the other. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Sardinia's armistice — signed against the Directory's orders: a king at his discretion. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We reached Acqui yesterday. Beaulieu flies so fast that we cannot catch him Send me a geographical, historical, political, and topographical note on the imperial fiefs in the neighbourhood of Genoa; also a note on the Dukes of Parma, Placentia, and Modena; the forces they have in the field; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Connoisseur's shopping list: notes on fiefs, dukes — and their pictures and statues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your answer. I beg you will express to the Corps Legislatif the thanks of the army for the honourable decree which it has voted; it is the most grateful recompense that the army can receive. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Thanks of the army voted; devotion to the constitution professed — for now. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army of Italy is in the greatest distress It is every day reinforcedy and its necessities increase in proportion. When the Directory gave me the command of this army it drew up a plan of offensive warfare necessitating prompt measures and extraordinary resources. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: An army in distress: pay months late, needs growing with every recruit. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As for myself, nothing can add to the esteem and devotion I have shown on all occasions to the constitution. I saw it established in the midst of the most revolting passions, PASSAGE OF THE PO. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Tortona, 1796-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 6,000 men which we defeated yesterday and obliged to recross the Adda, weaken him greatly. Another victory and we shall be masters of Italy If we had a good administrator we should be as well off as it is possible to imagine. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Carnot from Placentia, 1796-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “it will be as terrible as the fire from heaven towards rebels." Several comminatory articles follow, calculated to strike terror into the hearts of persons guilty of even speaking against France in private. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Inhabitants Of The Milanais, iZth, 1796-05-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Inhabitants Of The Milanais from Izth, 1796-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Augereau posts Rusca's brigade in Frugarolo, well guarded. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Rusca's brigade into Frugarolo, well guarded. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Augereau placera la brigade du général Rusca dans la ville de Frugarolo, bien gardée.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Beaumont bivouacs the cavalry left beyond Friugarolo village. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cavalry bivouacked left beyond Friugarolo toward Laharpe. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Beaumont bivouaquera la cavalerie, la gauche en arrière du village de Friugarolo.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Laharpe crosses the Scrivia at once with all and enters Tortona. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Cross the Scrivia at once with all, enter Tortona. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Laharpe de passer sur-le-champ la Scrivia avec toute sa division, et d'entrer à Tortone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send fifty chasseurs to Novi for fifteen thousand bread rations today. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Fifty chasseurs to Novi: fifteen thousand bread rations today. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Tu voudras bien faire partir cinquante chasseurs pour Novi, de te faire dans le jour quinze mille rations de pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Pelletier marches half his troops to Serravalle at once. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Half his troops to Serravalle castle at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Pelletier de partir avec la moitié des troupes pour Serravalle.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna seizes Bassignana boats, holds the right bank. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Guards on Bassignana boats, right bank held, none pass at Dozena. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Masséna enverra une garde pour s'emparer des barques de Bassignana, rive droite tenue.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter received, Sir, with thanks for the obliging intelligence. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Thanks for obliging intelligence, Monsieur. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu, Monsieur, la lettre que vous m'avez écrite. Je vous suis très-obligé des renseignements.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This despatch reached Bonaparte just after the victory of Lodi, and it is easy to imagine how deeply it irritated him. Instead, however, of braving the decision of the Government, as he might probably have done with impunity, he merely asked to be recalled. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Carnot from I4^A, 1796-05-04. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief is warned inhabitants were pillaged by horsemen. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Warned: inhabitants pillaged; Beaumont's horsemen guilty. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef est prévenu que beaucoup d'habitants ont été pillés par des cavaliers.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna floats every Tanaro boat down to Sale without delay. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Every Tanaro and Bassignana boat down to Sale without delay. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Masséna de faire descendre sans délai, vis-à-vis Sale, tous les bateaux du Tanaro.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Augereau suffers no Po communication; every boat stopped and seized. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: No Po communication; stop and seize every passing boat. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Augereau de ne souffrir aucune communication entre les deux rives du Pô, et d'arrêter tous les bateaux.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have at last crossed the Po. The second campaign has commenced. Beaulieu is disconcerted; he miscalculates, and continually falls into the snares I set for him. Perhaps he wishes to give battle, for he has both audacity and energy, but not genius. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content at the Po crossing (7 May). 'We have at last crossed the Po': the second campaign opens; Beaulieu wants genius. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have rushed Uke a torrent from the top of the Apennmes; you have overthrown and scattered all that opposed your march. Piedmont, delivered from Austrian tyranny, indulges her natural sentiments of peace and friendship towards France. Milan is yours, and the Republican flag waves throughout Lombardy. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Milan entered: the proclamation posted.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The nobles, priests, and agents of Austria lead the people of these splendid countries astray. The French army, as generous as it is strong, will treat all peaceful inhabitants with fraternity; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Dateline partly illegible in scan; placed by content amid the Milan proclamations (mid-May). Proclamation: fraternity for the peaceful — fire from heaven for rebels. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers, — You dashed like a torrent from the summit of the Apennines; you have overthrown, dispersed, and scattered all who opposed your march. " Piedmont, delivered from Austrian tyranny, has given vent to her natural sentiments of peace and friendship towards France. […]”
sourceTitle: To his brothers in arms, Milan, 1796-05-20
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: 'Milan is ours': the torrent from the Apennines proclaimed to the troops. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “'* The army which menaced you with such arrogance finds nothing to protect it against your courage. The Po, the Tessin, the Adda, did not stop you a single day; […]”
sourceTitle: To His Brothers In Arms, Milan, 1796-05-20
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to His Brothers In Arms from Milan, 1796-05-20. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. Commissioner Salicetti will forward you a list of the contributions we have imposed. You can at present count upon from 6,000,000 to 8,000,000 francs in gold or silver, ingots, or jewels which are at your disposal at Genoa at the house of one of the first bankers. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: War pays: 6–8 millions in gold, ingots and jewels at Genoa for Paris. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Brescia, May 28, 1796. Address to Soldiers During the Siege of Mantua, Nov. 6, 1796. Address to the Troops on the Conclusion of the First Italian Campaign, March, 1797. Address to the Genoese, 1797. Extract from a Letter to the Directory, April, 1797. Address to Soldiers after the Signing of the Treaty of Campo Formio, October, 1797. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Brescia entered.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is to deliver the finest country of Europe from the iron yoke of the arrogant house of Austria that the French army has braved the most difficult obstacles. Victory, in harmony with justice, has crowned these efforts. The remains of the enemy's army have fallen back behind the Mincio. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Republic of Venice, *' Brescia, 1796-05-29
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Entering Venetian land in pursuit — but remembering long friendship. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let the people have no anxiety, the severest I discipline shall be maintained, and everything furnished to the army shall be paid for in money. *'. Faithful in the road of honour, as in that of victory, the French soldier is terrible only for the enemies of hberty and of his Government. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Republic Of Venice, *' Brescia, 1796-05-29
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Republic Of Venice from *' Brescia, 1796-05-29. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They play and laugh with death; to-day they are quite accustomed to cavalry, and smile at it. Nothing can equal their intrepidity if it is not the gaiety with which they undertake forced marches; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Headquarters, 1796-06-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Here 100,000 spectators could sit down and hear easily all that an orator said. *'The emigres are flying from Italy; more than 1,500 left before our arrival. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Verona, 1796-06-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Engineers throw every means into Peschiera's fortifications, instantly. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Every engineering means into Peschiera fortifications, instantly. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le commandant du génie a ordre d'employer tous les moyens de l'art pour accroître les fortifications de Peschiera.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Adjutant Boyer rides to Castiglione-Mantovano to warn Augereau. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Boyer to Castiglione-Mantovano to warn Augereau. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: L'adjudant général Boyer partira pour Castiglione-Mantovano, où il trouvera le général Augereau.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Paris correspondence runs direct via Lyon, Chambéry, Turin. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Paris correspondence via Lyon-Chambéry-Turin direct. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: L'intention du général en chef étant d'établir la correspondance avec Paris par Lyon, Chambéry et Turin directement.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I reach this great beautiful city, leaving a good garrison. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Great and beautiful city held; good garrison masters it. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'arrive dans cette ville, qui est très-grande et très-belle. J'y laisse une bonne garnison.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sérurier sends an auxiliary officer to Roverbella headquarters at once. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Auxiliary officer to Roverbella headquarters at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Serurier d'envoyer sur-le-champ à Roverbella un des officiers auxiliaires.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Kilmaine sends all the 10th chasseurs to Roverbella headquarters. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: All the 10th chasseurs to Roverbella headquarters. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Kilmaine de faire partir tout le 10e chasseurs pour le quartier général à Roverbella.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Andréossy at Castiglione-Mantovano by 5 a.m. tomorrow. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. I–II — public domain (French)
context: Andréossy at Castiglione by 5 a.m. to catch the enemy. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au citoyen Andréossy d'être rendu demain, à cinq heures du matin, à Castiglione-Mantovano.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Augereau's division passed the Po yesterday and arrived at Bologna on the 19th; he found 400 soldiers of the Pope there and made them prisoners. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: A cardinal legate prisoner, four flags, and Parma's pictures claimed. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “he found 400 soldiers of the Pope there and made them prisoners. We have captured the Cardinal Legate, all the officers of the staff, and taken four flags; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from ^Bologna, 1796-06-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In order to make the Court of Rome tremble and feel that its magic has no effect on us, I have authorised the senate of Bologna to regard as null and void all the decrees violating its liberty. This has given great pleasure here and is severely felt at Rome. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Bologna, 1796-06-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There was little difficulty about the other conditions with the exception of the manuscripts; there, we were obliged to reduce our demands from 2,000 or 3,000 to 500 […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from *' Pistoja, 1796-06-26. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have sent them some fowling-pieces and barrels of powder, with twenty Corsican refugees belonging to the cantons which have shown the most energy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 6M, 1796-07-06. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have beaten the enemy. Kilmaine will send you the account. I am dead of fatigue. I entreat you to set out immediately for Verona. […] I give you a thousand kisses.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Roverbella, after the chase: beaten enemy, dead fatigue, Verona summoned. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have passed the whole night under arms. I should have taken Mantua by a bold and well directed blow, but the waters of the lake suddenly fell, and my columns, embarked, could not reach their landing-place. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Two hours after midnight at Marmirolo: a whole night under arms, Mantua missed. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “29 Messidor, year 4 [July 17, 1796). According to the last despatches from the general-inchief of the army of the Alps, citizen-general, it appears that he had not received the 200,000 francs in money which you have been charged to send him. […]”
sourceTitle: To the General-in-Chief: reply on Mantua, 1796-07-17
archive: Secret letters from Napoleon's cabinet (London, 1846), Vol. I — public domain
context: Paris answers Roverbella: Mantua's supplies will decide. Incoming voice: Paris orders to its general.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For two days I have had no letters from you. Thirty times to-day have I said this. You know therefore that I am very sad. You can not doubt the tender and absorbing solicitude with which you inspire me. We attacked Mantua yesterday. We bombarded it from two batteries with red-hot shot and shells. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Two days without her letters: thirty times counted in a day. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I hope that on arriving this evening, I shall receive one of your letters. You know, my dear Josephine, how much pleasure they give me. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Castiglione, 8 a.m.: hoping her letter arrives by evening. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The wants of the army require my presence in this region. It is impossible I should leave even to go to Milan. It would require five or six days. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: The army needs him: Milan must wait five or six days. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “4th, 45th and 5th line; 1st and 2nd of the 69th; light 17th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: New line-up: 4th, 45th, 5th; 69th's battalions; light 17th. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: 4e, 45e et 5e demi-brigade de ligne; 1er et 2e bataillon de la 69e et la 17e demi-brigade d'infanterie légère.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Kilmaine stays at Montechiaro with all his cavalry. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Kilmaine holds Montechiaro with all cavalry, watching right. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Kilmaine de rester à Montechiaro avec toute sa cavalerie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not think he (the Pope) will oppose the thunder of the Vatican against my thunder; and you will, I dare say, hear that I am at Rome in my barge. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Mrs. Nelson from Leghorn Roajys, 1796-08-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Thanks, however, to the victory of Lonato and to the vigorous measures I have adopted, matters will soon be set right. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Salicetti from ^^ Brescia, 1796-08-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You witnessed today's battles: 5,000 prisoners taken, many killed. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: You saw today's battles: 5,000 prisoners, many killed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous devez avoir été témoin des batailles données à l'ennemi aujourd'hui: nous lui avons pris 5,000 hommes, tué un grand nombre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Kilmaine details 100 grenadiers and 50 horse to march. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 100 grenadiers and 50 horse detailed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Kilmaine donnera des ordres pour que 100 grenadiers et un détachement de 50 chevaux marchent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Gaultier marches Bozzolo to Castenedolo at once. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Bozzolo to Castenedolo at once with all headquarters kit. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Gaultier de partir sur-le-champ de Bozzolo pour se rendre à Castenedolo.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Joubert at Castiglione delle Stiviere by six o'clock. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Castiglione delle Stiviere by six o'clock. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Joubert de partir pour se rendre à Castiglione delle Stiviere, où il devra être arrivé à six heures.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In entering a public career I adopted for principle, Everything for the country 1 […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Carnot from ^Verona, 1796-08-09. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My first thought is to write to you. Your health and your image have not been out of my mind for one moment during the whole way. I shall not be happy until I have received letters from you. I wait for them with impatience. It is not possible that you can realize my distress. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Brescia: first thought on arrival is her. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Vaubois note: Masséna reached Ala; tomorrow 8 or 9 a.m. she marches. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 4:30 p.m.: Masséna at Ala; tomorrow 8 or 9 she moves. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Vaubois est prévenu que la division du général Masséna est arrivée à Ala; que demain, à huit ou neuf heures du matin, elle se mettra en marche.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We are in full campaign, my adorable friend. We have overthrown the outposts of the enemy. […] The troops are in fine spirits, and well disposed. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Ala, in full campaign: outposts overthrown. English from the 1856 Confidential Correspondence (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If Naples is wanted, Citizen Directors, seriously consider reinforcements. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: If Naples is wanted, send reinforcements seriously. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Si vous voulez, Citoyens Directeurs, que l'on aille à Naples, songez sérieusement à m'envoyer des renforts.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna marches with all, artillery and 100 dragoons. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Whole division, artillery, 100 dragoons: leave at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Masséna de partir avec toute sa division, son artillerie et les 100 hommes du 15e dragons.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Milan sends all disposable cavalry to Peschiera at once. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: All Milan disposable cavalry to Peschiera at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général commandant à Milan fera partir au plus tôt pour Peschiera tout ce qui se trouve à Milan de disponible en cavalerie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Masséna marches tomorrow 22nd at 2 a.m. in greatest order. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: March the 22nd at 2 a.m. in greatest order. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne au général Masséna de partir, demain 22, à deux heures du matin, dans le plus grand ordre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Arrived here with all forces, chasing enemy posts. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 9:30 p.m.: arrived here with all forces, posts chased. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef me charge de vous prévenir que nous sommes arrivés ici, avec toutes nos forces, après en avoir chassé quelques postes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But should you ignore your own interests, and take up arms, we shall be terrible as the fire from heaven; we shall burn the houses and lay waste the territory of the villages which take part in a war that does not concern them. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Inhabitants Of The Tyrol, 14M, 1796-09-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Inhabitants Of The Tyrol from 14M, 1796-09-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your character, sir, which all who know you praise, induces me to permit you to return to Ferrara and to throw the veil of oblivion over your conduct of last month. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Cardinal Mattel from 26/A, 1796-09-26. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “These two forces united make 53,000 men, and at present we have only 27,000; cavalry, gunners, sappers, drivers, etc., were also needed, and If the preservation of Italy be dear to you, Citizen Directors, send me all this aid […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Milan, 1796-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “— ' I only wait for a favourable moment to fall upon Rome and to avenge the national honour. The chief object is to gain time The great art at present is to indulge in a little mutual recrimination in order to deceive that old fox. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Cardinal Mattel from Ferrara, 1796-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lombardy's people pronounce daily for us. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Lombardy pronounces daily; one great class waits to throw the glove. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le peuple de la Lombardie se prononce chaque jour davantage.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Majesté, l'Europe veut la paix. Cette guerre désastreuse dure depuis trop longtemps.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lombardy's people pronounce daily for us. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Lombardy pronounces daily. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le peuple de la Lombardie se prononce chaque jour davantage.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Majesty, Europe desires peace; this disastrous war lasted too long. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Majesté, l'Europe veut la paix. Cette guerre désastreuse dure depuis trop longtemps.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “they are all armed, and in some of the cantons the inhabitants are brave The King of Naples has raised a force of 60,000 men, and if he is to be attacked and dethroned that will require 18,000 infantry, and 3,000 cavalry Rome is strong owing to her fanaticism, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Milan, 1796-10-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it would be well to except — first, the four deputies who took the crown to London; second, the six members composing the Council of State of the Viceroy, and lastly the emigres I have caused citizen Panatieri, Paoli's secretary, who came from London to intrigue, to be arrested at Leghorn. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Verona, 1796-10-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Patrol Verona–Bassano against French soldiers' excesses. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Patrols Verona–Bassano against French pillagers. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous donnerez ordre qu'il soit fait des patrouilles sur la route de Vérone à Bassano, pour arrêter les excès des militaires français.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Transfer all unserviceable wounded to Lyon. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Unserviceable wounded to Lyon under war minister's orders. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'ordonner que tous les blessés hors d'état de servir soient transférés à Lyon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Modena's armistice conditions stand unfulfilled. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Modena's unpaid contribution had last term the 4th Messidor. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les conditions de l'armistice conclu avec le duc de Modène n'ont pas été remplies.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Modena's armistice conditions stand unfulfilled. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Modena's unpaid contribution had last term the 4th Messidor. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les conditions de l'armistice conclu avec le duc de Modène n'ont pas été remplies.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The siege of Mantua, sir, is more disastrous for humanity than two campaigns. Brave men ought to affront danger, but not the pestilence of a marsh. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Chivalry to the enemy: Mantua's marshes kill more surely than battles. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He compromised himself in '93 several times in spite of my reiterated advice. He wished to play the Jacobin. His sojourn at Marseilles would be dangerous for himself and the public weal as intriguers would get hold of him. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

context: Letter to The Directory from Zzth, 1797-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed: Lombardy independence proclamation. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Lombardy independent; executive installed; seat left vacant. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint la proclamation relative à l'indépendance de la Lombardie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Gallo showed Naples powers: Elba offered for the Levant isles. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Gallo showed Naples powers: Elba and Piombino offered for Levant isles. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: M. de Gallo m'a montré des pleins pouvoirs de Naples, offrant l'île d'Elbe contre les îles du Levant.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed intercepted Antraigues mail. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Intercepted Antraigues mail enclosed, No. I first. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint des lettres interceptées sur un courrier de M. d'Antraigues.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Pavia mobile column marches the 18th, sleeps at Milan. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Mobile column leaves Pavia the 18th, sleeps at Milan. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La colonne mobile qui est à Pavie en partira le 18 pour coucher à Milan.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Impatiently await the Venice marine inspection. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Inspect Venice marine impatiently; decide every hull's fate. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'attends avec impatience le résultat de l'inspection de la marine de Venise.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers — To-day is the anniversary of the 14th July. You see before you the names of your comrades who have fallen on the field of honour for the liberty of the country; they have furnished you with a brilliant example. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: 14 July order of the day: the fallen as example. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. The music for which you ask is being copied in the various towns of Italy. I shall take the greatest care to enrich the conservatory. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: The general with no soul for music writes to its inspectors. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Of all the fine arts, music is that which exercises the most influence on the passions — that which the legislator should most encourage. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Inspectors Of The Conservatory, Milan, 1797-07-26
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Inspectors Of The Conservatory from Milan, 1797-07-26. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Augereau has asked for permission to go to Paris, whither he is called by private affairs. I take the opportunity of forwarding the originals of the addresses to the army. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 27 Fa, 1797-07-27. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They are indignant to find doubt thrown upon the massacres of which they were victims. As for myself, I am engaged in endeavouring to restrain that patriotic ardour which is the distinctive character of all the soldiers of the army of Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 28M, 1797-07-28. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Attempts have been made to disturb your Royal Highness, and to invent motives for dispute between you and the French Republic. " I consider it my duty to inform your Royal Highness 77 that the Directory having every reason to be satisfied with the conduct of your Royal Highness during the whole of t […]”
sourceTitle: To the Grand Duke of Tuscany, Milan, 1797-08-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Tuscany settled from Milan. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “in my own name, having witnessed the reception and the care which your Royal Highness has always lavished on my brothers in arms, I shall always feel flattered at being able to be agreeable to you. To this feeling of gratitude must be joined a feeling of esteem. […]”
sourceTitle: To H.R.H. The Grand Duke Of Tuscany, Milan, 1797-08-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to H.R.H. The Grand Duke Of Tuscany from Milan, 1797-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have the honour of forwarding you a copy of the reply made by the Pope. If the Directory desires he will issue a pastoral letter directing the bishops to preach obedience to the laws of the Republic. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Minister Of Foreign Affairs, •' Milan, 1797-08-22
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Minister Of Foreign Affairs from •' Milan, 1797-08-22. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Glad His Majesty ordered the division reorganized. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Squadron news seen with pleasure; division reorganized. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai vu avec plaisir que Sa Majesté avait donné les ordres pour que la division fût réorganisée.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Press Rome to recognize the Cisalpine Republic. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Press Rome to recognize the Cisalpine, as Sardinia did. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de faire expliquer la cour de Rome et de la porter à reconnaître la République cisalpine.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 5th line leaves Venice for Tortona. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 5th line leaves Venice for Tortona; general follows. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Donner l'ordre à la 5e demi-brigade de ligne, qui est à Venise, d'en partir pour Tortone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Forwarding the finance minister's letter; print it. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Finance minister's letter communicated; print it. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai l'honneur de vous communiquer la lettre au ministre des finances; je désirerais qu'on l'imprimât.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" The sovereignty of the people, liberty, this," said the General-in-Chief, " is the political code of the Gospel. " Bonaparte.'* Bonaparte was quite as indignant with Naples as with Austria on the subject of her pretensions, and spoke and wrote as harshly of Acton as he did of Thugut. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Archbishop Of Genoa, ^* Passariano, 1797-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Archbishop Of Genoa from ^* Passariano, 1797-09-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think that henceforward the maxim of the Republic should be never to abandon Corfu, Zante, &c. We ought, on the contrary, to establish ourselves there firmly; we shall find immense resources there for our commerce, and they will be of great use to us in future European movements. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Corfu maxim: never abandon the Mediterranean.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “we shall find immense resources there for our commerce, and they will be of great use to us in future European movements. ' Why should we not seize upon the island of Malta? […]”
sourceTitle: To The Minister Of Foreign Affairs, Passariano, 1797-09-13
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Minister Of Foreign Affairs from Passariano, 1797-09-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The negotiations are almost broken off: the Austrians demand too much. ' Send me money with all diligence; dip into all the coffers for we must have some immediately; in twelve days we shall be campaigning. Look to the Brescians, I must have a million from them. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Haller from Passariano, 1797-10-06. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have not a single Italian in my army with the exception, I think, of 1,500 scamps, picked up in the 89 streets of various towns, who pillage and are good for nothing. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Foreign Minister from Passariano, 1797-10-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “To-day we proceeded to exchange the ratifications of the treaty of Campo Formio. All the members of the Congress have arrived and have paid me a visit. The King of Sweden has sent the Baron de Fersen as his ambassador. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: From Rastatt: peacemaking as power politics. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think you might leave 25,000 men in Italy, take 36,000 to England, and order the rest to Nice, Chambery, and Corsica. For the expedition to England we shall require: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from *^ Milan, 1797-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “No, sir; the French Republic will not tolerate men who are too well known by their liasons with the ancient court of France to come and brave the ministers of the first people on earth. During this discourse the Baron changed colour several times, but acted like a courtier. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Foreign Minister from Rastadt, 1797-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have given all the necessary orders for moving our column on the ocean. I shall send Citizen Andreossy to Paris to-morrow, in order to cast guns of the same calibre as the English field-pieces, so that, once in the country, we may be able to use their cannon balls. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 12M, 1797-11-12. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “*' No matter what post the Government assigns to the Army of Italy, it will always be worthy to sustain the liberty and glory of the French name. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Army from 14M, 1797-11-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In all the letters addressed to him, and which have been intercepted, I have found nothing out of conformity with the principles of the Republic. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Milan, 1797-11-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Cisalpine Republic, Nov. 17, 1797. " We have given you liberty. Take care you preserve it. To be worthy of your destiny make only discreet and honorable laws, and cause them to be executed with energy. Favor the diffusion of knowledge, and respect religion. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: A sister republic proclaimed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “To be free, the French people had kings to fight. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Return presentation, Campo Formio in his pocket. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le peuple français, pour être libre, avait les rois à combattre.

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “Enclosed, Citizen General, a copy of the secret convention between the French Republic and the Emperor. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Incoming voice: secret convention with the Emperor, execute in Italy. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint, Citoyen Général, une copie de la convention secrète conclue entre la République française et l'Empereur.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just received your works. Your pen is a paintbrush. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Napoleon the reader: your pen is a paintbrush. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je reçois à l'instant un exemplaire de vos ouvrages. Votre plume est un pinceau.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The votes of the distinguished men of the Institut honor me. Before being their equal I shall long be their schoolboy. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Elected to the Institut: long their schoolboy first. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le suffrage des hommes distingués qui composent l'Institut m'honore. Je sens bien qu'avant d'être leur égal je serai longtemps leur écolier.
